# The Unexpected Gift of Getting Lost

I got lost last week in a neighborhood I thought I knew well. My phone died—that modern prelude to disaster—and I found myself on a tree-lined street without the blue dot to guide me home. For exactly four minutes, I felt a flash of that old anxiety, the one that says we're incompetent without our devices. Then something shifted.

I noticed things. Really noticed them, the way you do when you're not moving fast, not moving toward something, just moving. There was a house with a blue door and flower boxes that seemed to be exploding with geraniums—the kind of meticulous care that speaks of someone who genuinely loves their home. A dog barked from behind a fence, and I could hear children laughing on a distant porch. The sun was beginning that golden hour descent, and the light was doing that thing it does in late afternoon where everything looks like it's been slightly filtered through honey.

I've walked down versions of this street dozens of times. I drive through this neighborhood regularly. But I had never *seen* it before.

This got me thinking about how we've engineered the entire experience of being lost out of human existence. We don't stumble onto new places anymore; we arrive at them. We don't discover; we navigate. There's something genuinely lost in that—and I mean that without irony—something about the particular texture of human experience that required getting lost sometimes.

I'm not about to become one of those people who romanticizes inconvenience or advocates for us all to abandon our phones and live in intentional obsolescence. That's not what I mean. But I wonder if we've lost the permission to be uncertain about our location, both literally and metaphorically. The pressure to have a destination, to be optimized in our movement through space and time, is relentless.

When I finally found my way home that afternoon, I came at it from an unexpected angle, through a park I didn't know existed three blocks away. It has a small pond with ducks and a playground that's actually well-maintained. There's a little community garden where people have written their names on the planters. It exists entirely parallel to my normal routes, invisible to me despite its proximity. For months, maybe years, it's been there, and I never knew.

This makes me think about how many invisible parks we're walking past in every aspect of our lives. How many unexpected connections we're missing because we've optimized ourselves right past them. How many conversations we won't have because we've got our route planned. How many moments of discovery have been replaced with moments of arrival.

I've been thinking a lot lately about the difference between having experiences and collecting them. There's a quality of tourism that has crept into how we live, even in our own lives. We move from thing to thing, checking boxes, accumulating memories like we're filling a suitcase. Did I experience it fully? Did I take a good photo? Did I understand it? Do I have the right feelings about it? It's exhausting just describing it.

But when I was lost last week—genuinely uncertain, without the ability to verify my location on a screen—I wasn't in collection mode. I was in presence mode. I couldn't optimize for the experience because I didn't know what the experience was. I was just walking, observing, noticing. The geraniums weren't a detail I could screenshot and caption later. They were just geraniums, and they were beautiful, and that was enough.

There's a passage in a book I read years ago—I can't remember which one, which is perhaps its own kind of lesson—where the author talks about how modern life has given us unprecedented ability to curate our experience of the world, and how this curation is slowly killing something essential about being human. We choose what we see, what we read, who we listen to. We build these perfect bubbles of information that reflect our existing beliefs back to us. And the author's point was that getting lost in the world—whether that's literally wandering a street or intellectually stumbling onto an idea that challenges you—is how we grow.

I think about how much friction we've removed from our lives. We've tried to optimize every surface, every process, every relationship into something smooth and efficient. And smoothness is not, it turns out, the same thing as good. Smoothness is sometimes boring. Smoothness is sometimes deadening. Smoothness can sometimes feel like moving through a world made of plastic.

The friction of getting lost, of uncertainty, of not knowing exactly what comes next—that friction is where interesting things happen. That's where you notice the geraniums. That's where you find the hidden park. That's where you realize you've been walking past wonder for months and didn't even know it.

I think this is why I'm growing increasingly allergic to advice that claims to have it all figured out. The productivity tips, the life optimization strategies, the five-step plans to happiness. None of them account for the value of the unplanned moment, the unexpected turn, the beautiful thing you'd see if you just looked around without a GPS destination lodged in your brain.

What if the good life isn't about having better navigation? What if it's about being willing to be a little lost?

Last Sunday, I went back to the park I found. I sat by the pond for an hour. I read the names on the community garden planters. I watched a child feed ducks while his mother sat on a bench reading. Nothing happened. There was no destination, no purpose beyond being there. It was probably the most productive hour of my week because it was the only hour where I wasn't trying to produce anything.

I'm not claiming to have it figured out. That would be the ultimate irony—optimizing how to be unoptimized. But I'm noticing how good it feels to move through the world a little slower, a little less certain, a little more open to the possibility of geraniums.

Sometimes the best place to arrive is the place you didn't mean to go.
